t:
Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act of 1940 (15 U.S.C. 80a–46(b)) is amended to read as follows:

“(b)(1) 
A contract that is made, or whose performance involves, a violation of this title, or of any rule, regulation, or order thereunder, is unenforceable by either party (or by a nonparty to the contract who acquired a right under the contract with knowledge of the facts by reason of which the making or performance violated or would violate any provision of this title or of any rule, regulation, or order thereunder) unless a court finds that under the circumstances enforcement would produce a more equitable result than nonenforcement and would not be inconsistent with the purposes of this title.


“(2) 
To the extent that a contract described in paragraph (1) has been performed, a court may not deny rescission at the instance of any party unless such court finds that under the circumstances the denial of rescission would produce a more equitable result than its grant and would not be inconsistent with the purposes of this title.


“(3) 
This subsection shall not apply (A) to the lawful portion of a contract to the extent that it may be severed from the unlawful portion of the contract, or (B) to preclude recovery against any person for unjust enrichment.”.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that the references to a "rule, regulation, or order" and to court findings signal rulemaking or a right to sue. That fails because the section only governs the enforceability and rescission of private contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, in disputes between private parties. It neither grants new rulemaking authority nor creates a right to sue or object to a federal decision, and it provides no consultation, hearing, or advisory process involving outside parties.
fable.s: is unenforceable by either party (or by a nonparty to the contract who acquired a right under the contract with knowledge of the facts

opus.w: The provision decides whether private contracts that violate the Investment Company Act can be enforced or rescinded, and courts make that call between private parties. No outside party is consulted on a federal decision, given a right to challenge one, or invited to comment. The mention of 'rule, regulation, or order' refers to existing rules and does not authorize new rulemaking, so it is not participation.
opus.s: A contract that is made, or whose performance involves, a violation of this title, or of any rule, regulation, or order thereunder, is unenforceable by either party
opus.b: This section is not participation. The tempting reading is that it involves participation because it mentions courts, rescission suits, and "any rule, regulation, or order thereunder." That fails for two reasons. The litigation is between private parties to a contract, not an outside party challenging a federal decision. And the reference to rules only points to existing ones; it doesn't grant new rulemaking authority.

qwen_chat.w: This section defines the legal enforceability of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act and the equitable powers of courts to grant or deny rescission. It does not require the federal government to consult with, coordinate with, or receive input from outside parties (such as the public, states, or experts) before making a decision. The involvement of courts and private parties here is related to litigation and contract enforcement, which falls under the exclusion for 'limiting or describing litigation' rather than granting a right to participate in a federal decision-making process.
qwen_chat.s: A contract that is made, or whose performance involves, a violation of this title, or of any rule, regulation, or order thereunder, is unenforceable by either party... unless a court finds that under the circumstances enforcement would produce a more equitable result than nonenforcement
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that because the text mentions "a court" and "rescission," it involves outside parties (litigants) interacting with the government or legal system. However, the definition explicitly states that "a court's jurisdiction, venue, or the statute-of-limitations period for suits - limiting or describing litigation is not the same as GRANTING an outside party a right to sue a decision." This section defines the enforceability of contracts and the equitable powers of courts in private disputes or enforcement actions, but it does not establish a process for the federal government to consult with or coordinate with outside parties before making a regulatory or administrative decision. It is a substantive rule about contract law, not a procedural requirement for public participation in government decision-making.
